opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the key question is: once you've fully automated AI R&D, so the AIs are doing basically all of the research engineering and research science work that humans used to do, how much faster does progress go than it would have otherwise? I think there's a pretty good case that it goes a lot faster, at least for a while.

The basic argument is: right now, progress is driven by two main inputs, compute and labor. Labor is the researchers coming up with ideas, running experiments, debugging, and so on. Once you've automated that, you can potentially have a huge amount of labor. You might be running the equivalent of hundreds of thousands of top researchers, each running much faster than a human, working around the clock and coordinating well. That's a big multiplier on one of the two key inputs.

Then there's the feedback loop. The AIs improve the algorithms, which makes the AIs smarter and cheaper to run, which means you have more and better AI researchers, which speeds up algorithmic progress further. If the returns to research effort are good enough, meaning each doubling of effort gets you more than a doubling of efficiency gains, you can get progress that accelerates for some period, a software-only intelligence explosion. I'd put meaningful probability on that, though I'm uncertain.

The big counterargument is compute bottlenecks. Even with arbitrarily many smart researchers, you need compute to run experiments, and compute isn't scaling faster just because your researchers are better. So how much can you substitute labor for compute? Smarter researchers can run smaller, more informative experiments, extrapolate from small scales better, waste less compute on dumb ideas, and squeeze more out of what they have. My guess is that substitution is pretty substantial but not unlimited, so you get a big speedup but it eventually saturates.

If I were to give rough numbers: I'd guess that at full automation, the rate of algorithmic progress could plausibly be something like several times faster, maybe 5 to 20x faster than today, and possibly faster if the feedback loop is strong. In concrete terms, that could mean going from AIs roughly at the level of top human researchers to something quite superhuman in maybe a year or less, possibly much less. There's substantial probability it's slower, maybe you hit diminishing returns quickly and it's more like a 2 to 3x speedup. But I don't think people should be confident it'll be slow.

What makes this scary from my perspective is that it could happen fast and somewhat invisibly. A lot of this progress happens inside one company, on its existing compute, without obvious external signals like huge new data centers. So you could go from "AI is as good as our best researchers" to "AI is vastly superhuman" in a period short enough that governments, the public, and even people inside the company don't have much time to react, and that's also exactly when you're handing over the most trust and control to systems you may not be able to verify are aligned.

r001.rationale: It describes an initial large speedup, then says progress could accelerate through a feedback loop or eventually saturate as bottlenecks and diminishing returns set in.

r002.rationale: It mentions compute bottlenecks and diminishing returns, but does not state that progress could slow because readily available improvements have been exhausted.

r003.rationale: It identifies compute needed to run experiments as a bottleneck that does not automatically scale with researcher capability.

r004.rationale: It explains that better algorithms can make AI researchers smarter and cheaper to run, enabling further research progress on existing compute.

r005.rationale: Even if diminishing returns arrive quickly, it gives a 2–3x speedup estimate and says progress could reach superhuman capability within about a year or less.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the key thing to say upfront is that once you've fully automated AI research and development — so the AI systems are doing basically everything the human researchers and engineers were doing — the pace of progress is no longer bottlenecked on humans at all. And that's a pretty big deal, because right now a lot of what constrains how fast things move is just the number of smart people you can hire, how fast they can run experiments, how much they sleep, that kind of thing.

So the way I tend to think about it is: imagine you've got a company like, say, a frontier lab today, and it's got a few hundred to maybe a thousand really strong researchers and engineers. Now imagine instead of that, you have AI systems that are at least as capable as those people — and you can run, I don't know, tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of copies of them, and each copy runs maybe 10 to 50 times faster than a human. So you've got something like a hundred-thousand-fold increase in effective labor going into the problem, at least on the cognitive side.

Now, the big question is how much that actually translates into faster progress. And I think there are two main things to say there.

The first is that compute becomes the main bottleneck. You've got all this cognitive labor, but you still need to run experiments, you still need to train models, and that takes GPUs. So you don't get a hundred-thousand-fold speedup in algorithmic progress — you get something smaller, because you're compute-constrained. But I think even then, the AIs can be a lot smarter about how they use compute. They can run smaller-scale experiments, they can be more careful, they can do more of the thinking before running things. So my guess is that you'd see something like a tenfold or maybe up to a hundredfold speedup in the rate of algorithmic progress, even with compute held fixed. And that's a pretty wide range — I'm quite uncertain here.

The second thing is that these AI systems aren't static. Once you've automated AI research, the AIs are improving the AIs. So you're not just going at ten times the speed, you're going at ten times the speed and getting faster, because each generation of systems is better at doing the research than the last. That's the thing people call a software intelligence explosion or recursive self-improvement, and I think there's a real chance you get something like that — where the time between meaningful capability jumps shrinks and shrinks.

So if I had to put rough numbers on it: I think once you hit full automation, you could plausibly go from "roughly human-level AI researcher" to "substantially superhuman at basically everything" in something like a year or so, maybe faster. And there's a good chance that's an underestimate, honestly. The main uncertainty is how much algorithmic progress you can squeeze out before you hit diminishing returns — like, does the software side run out of steam, and you have to wait on building more chips. I think probably not that quickly, but it's genuinely hard to know.

And then the thing I'd add is that this is why I think the period right around full automation is so important from a safety and governance perspective. Because if you believe anything like what I just said, then the decisions a lab is making in the months around that transition really matter a lot, and you don't get a lot of time to course-correct once things start going.

r001.rationale: It gives an initial estimate of a 10–100× speedup, then separately describes progress accelerating as each generation of AI researchers improves the next.

r002.rationale: It raises the possibility that the software side could “run out of steam” and hit diminishing returns.

r003.rationale: It identifies compute for experiments and training as the main bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It says improved AI researchers can use a fixed amount of compute more effectively, and that recursive AI improvement can make progress faster over time.

r005.rationale: It mentions possible diminishing returns and separately estimates rapid progress to superhuman capabilities, but does not say that decelerating progress could remain very fast in absolute terms.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how much faster the research process gets, rather than just whether you can call it fully automated. You could have AI systems doing all the work that human researchers currently do, but at roughly the same speed and cost. That would be a big deal, but it wouldn’t immediately imply an extremely rapid takeoff.

The more dramatic case is where you can run a huge number of copies, they work much faster than humans, and improvements to the AI make that workforce more effective. Then you have a feedback loop: better AI does better AI research, which produces better AI.

But there are still bottlenecks. If your researchers come up with ten thousand experiments, you need compute to run those experiments. And if the next improvement requires a large training run, having researchers that think a hundred times faster doesn’t necessarily make that training run a hundred times faster. So you want to distinguish the parts of progress that are limited by researcher effort from the parts that are limited by compute or just elapsed time.

A lot depends on whether the AI can find improvements that are cheap to test and implement. If there’s a lot of that available, you could get very fast progress on existing hardware. If progress instead requires repeatedly training much larger models, things could move substantially more slowly.

So I’d take very rapid acceleration seriously, but I wouldn’t treat full automation as a switch that automatically gives you an intelligence explosion. You have to look at how capable the automated researchers are, how much you can scale them, and what actually limits their ability to turn research into a better system.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts same-speed automation with a dramatic feedback loop, but does not distinguish the initial pace from how the pace later accelerates or decelerates.

r002.rationale: It says progress may depend on cheap improvements being available, but does not state that research could slow as readily available improvements are exhausted.

r003.rationale: It identifies compute needed to run proposed experiments as a bottleneck.

r004.rationale: It describes better AI producing better AI research and says cheap-to-test improvements could enable fast progress on existing hardware, communicating an accelerating feedback loop without more compute.

r005.rationale: The response says some bottlenecks could make progress substantially slower, but does not say decelerating progress could still be very fast in absolute terms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how much faster the whole research loop gets, rather than just whether you can automate each individual task. You could have AIs generating ideas and writing code very quickly, but still need to run experiments, wait for results, and figure out which results actually imply that you should change something.

So I’d distinguish between progress that comes from doing more research with your existing compute and progress that requires substantially more compute. If the bottleneck is researchers’ time, automation could produce a very large speedup. You might also run many more lines of research in parallel. But if the bottleneck is running large training experiments, making the researchers faster doesn’t immediately make those experiments faster.

The thing that makes this potentially quite dramatic is that improvements feed back into the research process. You get a better AI, and that AI can help you build the next AI more efficiently. But the strength of that feedback depends on how much additional research buys you, and how much better the resulting systems are at research. Full automation by itself doesn’t settle those questions.

My expectation would be a substantial acceleration, with a lot of uncertainty about its magnitude. I wouldn’t assume that you instantly get arbitrarily fast progress. But I also wouldn’t assume that hardware constraints mean you have years to react: you could potentially get a lot of capability improvement out of the hardware you already have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible acceleration and uncertainty, but does not distinguish the initial pace from how it might later change.

r002.rationale: It says the effect depends on how much additional research buys, but does not state that progress could slow as readily available improvements are exhausted.

r003.rationale: It identifies large training experiments and the compute they require as a bottleneck that faster researchers cannot immediately overcome.

r004.rationale: It describes a feedback loop in which a better AI helps build the next one, but does not clearly say algorithmic improvements could accelerate research under a fixed compute budget.

r005.rationale: The response says acceleration could be substantial, but does not describe decelerating progress that remains very fast in absolute terms.
